To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
multiple displacement amplification (Mda) is a technique that can be used to investigate human papillomaviruses (Hpv).
MDA can be used to amplify HPV DNA from tiny amounts of tissue and that it can be used to investigate HPV physical status.
MDA has the potential to assist in investigations of HPV integration in cervical cancer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of MDA in the study of human papilloma virus (HPV) integration.
the use of MDA in the investigation of the physical status of HPV in human cancers.
the use of multiple displacement ampliﬁcation in the investigation of the physical status of human papilloma virus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MDA has been successfully used to detect integrated HPV in a variety of samples, and is therefore a valuable addition to the armamentarium of HPV research.

multiple displacement amplification (a phi29 polymerase based whole genomic amplification technique) has the potential to assist in HPV physical status investigation, by yielding large amounts (>40 μg), high molecular weight DNA, from tiny starting quantities (50 ng).
the use of MDA is not a problem, it is an advantage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MDA has potential to be a useful tool for HPV studies.
MDA can be used to investigate HPV physical status in solid tumours and in cytological samples.
the MDA technique is a useful tool for the investigation of HPV in pre-invasive and invasive cervical lesions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
MDA is a powerful tool for the study of HPV physical status in clinical samples.
MDA can be used to detect integrated HPV in clinical specimens, which will be important for the development of HPV-based therapies.
MDA can generate sufficient DNA from small samples for the investigation of the HPV physical status in cervical cancer and precursors.
